Register a hotkey that brings iTerm2 to the foreground when you're in another application. A terminal is always a keypress away.
iTerm2 comes with a robust find-on-page feature. The UI stays out of the way. All matches are immediately highlighted. Even regular expression support is offered!
Just type the start of any word that has ever appeared in your window and then Cmd-; will pop open a window with suggestions.

Paste history lets you revisit recently copied or pasted text. You can even opt to have the history saved to disk so it will never be lost.
Instant replay lets you travel back in time to recover text that was erased from the terminal.

you can have iTerm2 switch profiles depending on what you're doing. For example, you can define a profile that's always used when you ssh to some hostname.
iTerm2 has a custom escape sequence to display images right in the terminal. Even animated GIFs!

When you run "tmux -CC", a new tmux session is created. An iTerm2 window opens and it acts like a normal iTerm2 window. The difference is that when iTerm2 quits or the ssh session is lost, tmux keeps running.
iTerm2 offers a Python package which makes it easy to write Python scripts that control iTerm2 and extend its behavior.
iTerm2 has sophisticated AppleScript support allowing one to write stand-alone scripts to launch the application and open multiple sessions with profiles into either new tabs or new windows.
This is an optional component you can install to enable generative AI features in iTerm2.
Browser profiles integrate web browsing into iTerm2's window/tab/pane hierarchy. Copy mode, triggers, AI chat, and other terminal features work in browser sessions.
Triggers - Regex patterns that fire actions when matched: highlight text, run commands, send notifications, open password manager, set marks, or invoke Python scripts.
Smart Selection - Quad-click selects semantic objects (URLs, file paths, email addresses, quoted strings). Right-click for context actions. Cmd-click to open.

Session Restoration - Sessions run in long-lived server processes. If iTerm2 crashes or upgrades, your shells keep running. When iTerm2 restarts, it reconnects to your sessions exactly where you left off.
Open Quickly - Cmd-Shift-O opens a search across all sessions by tab title, command, hostname, directory, or badge. Navigate large session collections instantly.
iTerm2 supports user-defined triggers, which are actions that run when text matching a regular expression is received.

Search all your tabs at once with Global Search.
When iTerm2 quits or the ssh session is lost, tmux keeps running. You can return to the host you were ssh'ed into and run "tmux -CC attach" and the iTerm2 windows will reopen in the same state
iTerm2 is a replacement for Terminal and the successor to iTerm.

"It takes much less effort for me to simply switch back to Terminal.app." (reacting to iTerm2 adding an opt-in OpenAI-based AI feature)

Users reported that iTerm2's new AI feature wasn't a true disabled toggle: "Put anything in the box for the OpenAI key, valid or not, and the functionality to send data to OpenAI is active. Accidentally put a [space] in that box and it looks like there is nothing there."
Some users called the backlash overblown: "a feature that is inactive by default, consumes no processing power, memory or anything else" still caused the developer to be "bullied."

Discussion of an iTerm2 vulnerability where 'cat'-ing a file could hide unprintable/escape characters that manipulate the terminal; fix was committed upstream but hadn't yet reached stable releases at time of disclosure.

"imgcat: you can view images without leaving your terminal. Somehow this works even across SSH connections… Python scripting API: basically AppleScript for iTerm except it lets you touch pretty much everything and it's not soul-crushing to write."
"Along with imgcat there's it2dl. Downloads a file from the remote system browser-style. It's much more convenient than scp, especially when several sessions deep."
"Semantic History is pretty handy and not well-known. It lets you Command+Click on a path to open it in your editor (or associated application)."
"I'm a little jealous of iTerm, not going to lie. The UX is pretty nice from what I've seen, but I can't find a like for like replacement for either Windows or Linux."
